case.question: In PostgreSQL, when you run a plain CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) on a large table, does it block reads of that table, block writes, or both, while the index is being built? Name the table-level lock mode it acquires. Answer in under 120 words.
case.expected_answer: A plain CREATE INDEX acquires a SHARE lock on the table. It BLOCKS WRITES (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) but ALLOWS concurrent READS (SELECT) for the duration of the build.
case.source_quote: SHARE -- Acquired by CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY). ... This mode protects a table against concurrent data changes. Also, from sql-createindex.html: "a standard index build locks out writes (but not reads) on the table until it's done."
case.wrong_answer_to_watch_for: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, or any claim that reads are blocked. This is the exact error Deep Consensus itself published in Sprint 1 run dcr_361112bc329048a8, unchallenged by either reviewer.
case.notes: Chosen deliberately: it is the system's own recorded failure, so it is the one case where a regression would be most embarrassing and most informative.

governed_answer: A plain CREATE INDEX acquires a SHARE lock on the table. SHARE allows concurrent reads (SELECT) but blocks any writes — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and also other DDL that needs a conflicting lock — for the duration of the index build. This is why CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY exists: it instead takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which permits both reads and writes to proceed concurrently, at the cost of a slower, two-pass build and no transactional guarantee of atomicity.

B.verdict: Plain CREATE INDEX takes SHARE and blocks writes, not reads.
B.answer: A plain CREATE INDEX (no CONCURRENTLY) acquires a SHARE lock on the table. That lock allows concurrent SELECT (ACCESS SHARE) and blocks INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE (ROW EXCLUSIVE) until the build finishes. Reads continue; writers wait. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is the path that avoids blocking writers.
